Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' 
(CMS) proposed rule, â€œCMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugsâ€ (CMS-0062-P). 
Prime Therapeutics LLC (Prime) is a pharmacy solutions partner that delivers savings, simplicity and

Prime also endorses the comments submitted by the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association

I. CMS Should Extend the October 1, 2027 Compliance Date for Medical-Benefit Drug 
Prior Authorization (Proposed Â§ II.B.3) 
Prime supports the policy intent of the FHIR API framework for medical-benefit drugs but cautions that an 
October 1, 2027, deadline is operationally challenging without additional implementation time. Because 
CMS-0062-P would apply the FHIR Prior Authorization API framework to medical-benefit drug prior 
authorization for the first time, we ask CMS to adopt a compliance timeline tied to finalization of the drug 
prior authorization implementation requirements, allowing for at least a 15-month implementation window 
after those requirements are finalized. 
Based on Prime's operational experience, incorporating medical-benefit drug prior authorization into the 
FHIR Prior Authorization API will require 9 to 15 months of build effort from the date the drug prior 
authorization implementation requirements are finalized, and operational responsibilities are agreed upon 
between Prime and its health plan clients. The scope of engineering work, including substantial IT 
investment costs estimated at up to $2 million, reflects the complexity of categorizing medical-benefit 
drugs, where a single drug may be administered through different routes and trigger different benefit 
categorizations, coverage logic, and prior authorization workflows. Compressing this work into an 
insufficient timeline increases the risk of misrouted PA requests, misapplied coverage logic, delayed 
beneficiary access to medically necessary medication, and inappropriate denials that disrupt ongoing 
therapy. 
CMS-0057-F established the Prior Authorization API framework for non-drug items and services, while 
expressly excluding covered outpatient and medical-benefit drugs from its API and operational 
requirements. CMS-0062-P now proposes to extend elements of that framework to drug prior 
authorization. Because CMS is proposing newly mandated implementation guide versions and 
operational metrics for a category previously excluded from the 2024 final rule, delegated entities cannot 
reliably complete end-to-end system builds until these specific requirements are finalized. Compressing 
the finalization of drug-specific standards and operational implementation into an overlapping window 
creates operational risk, threatening care continuity for the vulnerable Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP 
beneficiaries the rule is intended to protect. 
We request that CMS extend the compliance date for incorporating medical-benefit drug prior 
authorization into the FHIR Prior Authorization API (Proposed Â§ II.B.3) to a date no earlier than 15 
months following publication of final implementation guidance. As an alternative, CMS could 
provide enforcement discretion during the first year of compliance to allow for the operational 
maturation of the framework. 
II. NCPDP Standards Adoption Should Be Calibrated to Ecosystem Readiness (Proposed 
Â§ II.A.2) 
Prime supports CMS's adoption of NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary and Benefit (F&B), and Real-Time 
Prescription Benefit (RTPB) as the standards for prescription drug prior authorization, formulary data 
exchange, and real-time benefit transparency. These standards reflect mature industry consensus, and 
Prime is positioned to support all three. However, the three standards differ materially in their current 
state of ecosystem readiness, particularly for non-Part D programs.

A. SCRIPT Standard (Proposed Â§Â§ II.A.2.a, II.B.4) 
Prime supports the use of NCPDP SCRIPT across all of its pharmacy-benefit lines of business, including 
Medicare Part D, Medicaid managed care, CHIP, QHP, and commercial.  
B. Formulary and Benefit Standard (Proposed Â§Â§ II.A.2.b, II.B.5) 
Prime supports the NCPDP F&B Standard Version 60 by January 2027. However, the successful rollout 
of this standard depends on precise version alignment across the entire healthcare ecosystem including 
alignment with the FHIR Implementation Guide versions cited in the Proposed Rule (i.e., Da Vinci PDex 
2.1.0, CARIN Blue Button 2.2.0, and related guides). The Proposed Rule's strict version-locking requires 
ecosystem-wide coordination across payers, vendors, and EHRs to deliver the standardized formulary 
and benefit data exchange the rule envisions. 
Prime also cautions that specifying standards at an overly granular version level within the regulatory text 
risks dating the rule. If a newer version of an adopted standard is published after the final rule takes 
effect, overly specific version-locking could prevent or delay industry adoption of the improved standard 
until a future rulemaking cycle catches up. Prime encourages CMS to build flexibility into the final rule. 
For example, by adopting a named standard while permitting subsequently published, backward-
compatible versions, or by establishing a streamlined process for recognizing updated versions so that 
the framework can incorporate standards improvements without requiring full notice-and comment 
rulemaking for each new version. 
We recommend CMS publish detailed implementation guidance for the NCPDP F&B Standard, 
including version specifications and compatibility requirements, with sufficient lead time before 
the compliance date to enable coordinated industry adoption across the payer-vendor-EHR 
network. We further recommend that CMS adopt a mechanism allowing recognition of newer 
published versions of adopted standards without requiring additional rulemaking, so that the 
framework keeps pace with standards development. 
C. Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard (Proposed Â§Â§ II.A.2.c, II.B.6) 
Prime supports the adoption of NCPDP RTPB Standard Version 13 in the Medicare Part D context, 
where the standard is mature, vendor support is in place, and prescriber-side adoption has reached 
meaningful scale.  
RTPB adoption is materially less mature, however, for non-Part D programs, particularly Medicaid. Three 
structural factors contribute to this readiness gap and warrant CMS's careful consideration: 
â€¢ 
Benefit Complexity: State-level variability in Preferred Drug Lists (PDLs), supplemental rebates, 
and MCO carve-outs require highly complex, state-specific response logic that does not exist in 
the Part D environment. 
â€¢ 
Reduced Value Proposition: Because Medicaid member cost-sharing is minimal or non-
existent, there has been significantly less investment from MCOs and EHR vendors in building 
the RTPB workflows that typically drive lower-cost alternative selection.

â€¢ 
Provider Fragmentation: Medicaid populations are often served by smaller, independent, or 
safety-net practices whose EHR systems lag far behind large health systems in RTPB activation. 
For Medicaid in particular, an October 1, 2027, compliance date assumes that payer-side, MCO-side, 
state-side, and prescriber/EHR-side capabilities will all reach functional alignment within approximately 
18 months of rule finalization. Based on current adoption patterns, this expectation may not be realistic. A 
compliance timeline that does not account for the multi-stakeholder nature of RTPB ecosystem readiness 
will produce technical compliance without functional delivery of the real-time benefit transparency CMS 
intends. 
Additionally, Prime cautions that RTPB is an "ecosystem standard." Payer-side compliance alone cannot 
deliver transparency if the prescriber-side EHR has not implemented the standard. Prime recommends 
CMS decouple the Medicaid RTPB compliance timeline from Part D. A phased approach or an extended 
implementation window for Medicaid is necessary to allow for EHR vendor alignment with safety-net 
provider workflows; state-level logic integration for complex benefit designs; and cross-stakeholder 
testing to ensure data accuracy before go-live. 
We request CMS adopt a phased compliance approach for the NCPDP RTPB Standard, with full 
compliance required for Medicare Part D and QHP programs by October 1, 2027, consistent with 
the Proposed Rule, and an extended compliance window of 24 additional months for Medicaid 
and CHIP programs to allow for ecosystem-wide adoption alignment. 
III. The Drug PA Decision Clock Should Run from Receipt of All Information Necessary for 
a Determination (Proposed Â§ II.C.3) 
Prime supports CMS's policy direction toward shorter, more responsive drug prior authorization decision 
timeframes. Timely decisions improve patient access and reduce uncertainty for prescribers and patients 
alike. Prime's pharmacy benefit operations already accommodate 24-hour expedited PA turnaround 
across all drug categories where expedited review is requested. Primeâ€™s average pharmacy benefit drug 
prior authorization decision time from May 2025 through May 2026 was approximately 0.57 days, or 13.7 
hours, across lines of business and request urgency. Prime, therefore, does not have substantive 
operational concerns with the decision-timeframe durations proposed in the rule. Prime does, however, 
recommend one specific clarification to the clock-start language to ensure that the framework actually 
delivers the timely-decision benefit CMS intends, rather than producing avoidable denials, appeals, and 
administrative cycles that consume more time than the decision they would otherwise have produced. 
As drafted, the Proposed Rule's decision timeframes run from receipt of the prior authorization request. 
In Primeâ€™s operational experience, some prior authorization requests require outreach to the prescriber 
for additional information before a determination can be made. The clinical information necessary for a 
medically appropriate determination, including diagnosis specificity, documentation of prior therapies, lab 
values, and clinical justification for non-formulary or step-therapy exception requests is often incomplete 
in initial submissions. Primeâ€™s own operational data confirm this: a meaningful share of drug prior 
authorization reviews require outbound research to obtain the information necessary for a determination, 
and critically, a substantial portion of those cases are ultimately approved once the requested information

is received. If the decision clock were required to run from initial receipt regardless of whether necessary 
clinical information had been submitted, these ultimately granted requests would face a higher risk of 
denial for lack of information, followed by resubmission or appeal once the missing information is 
provided.  
For Primeâ€™s pharmacy benefit prior authorization requests received from January 2026 through May 
2026, approximately 15 percent of Medicaid reviews and 30 percent of Medicare reviews required 
outbound research to obtain information necessary for a determination. Of the cases requiring research, 
approximately 35 percent of Medicaid cases and 37 percent of Medicare cases resulted in a granted 
decision following that outreach. These data illustrate that incomplete initial submissions are not merely 
an administrative inconvenience; they are often cases in which the missing information materially affects 
the outcome. 
Provider response times to outreach are influenced by factors outside the payer's or PBM's control. On 
the medical-benefit side in particular, provider-administered drug authorizations are typically prescribed 
by specialists whose offices maintain specialist hours and may be closed nights, weekends, holidays, 
and certain weekday afternoons. Requiring decisions on initial requests within tightly constrained 
windows running from the receipt of the request does not accelerate care in these scenarios. Instead, it 
produces denials that the prescriber will then appeal once the outstanding information is provided, 
creating administrative cycles that consume more time overall than a decision deferred until the 
necessary information is received. 
A modest drafting change resolves this concern without weakening the rule's timeliness objective. 
Changing the clock-start trigger from â€œreceipt of the requestâ€ to â€œreceipt of all information necessary for a 
determinationâ€ preserves CMS's interest in timely decision-making while avoiding the denial-and-appeal 
cycle that the current language would produce. 
We recommend CMS amend Proposed Â§ II.C.3 to specify that drug prior authorization decision 
timeframes begin upon receipt by the impacted payer of all information necessary for a 
determination, rather than upon initial receipt of the request. 
IV. Public Reporting of Drug PA Metrics Should Provide Adequate Implementation Time 
and Consideration of an Avoided-PA Measure (Proposed Â§ II.C.7) 
Prime supports CMS's policy direction toward public reporting of drug prior authorization performance 
metrics. Transparency into PA approvals, denials, decision times, extensions, and appeal outcomes 
provides plan beneficiaries, prescribers, and policymakers with meaningful information about how the 
prior authorization system functions. Two refinements would improve the durability and usefulness of the 
reporting framework. 
A. The Compliance Date for Public Posting of Drug PA Metrics Should Be Extended 
While Prime supports the drug PA metrics framework in principle, we strongly recommend that CMS 
provide additional time before public reporting of drug PA metrics is required. The Proposed Rule 
introduces new categorical definitions, new aggregation rules, and new data flows that have not been

operationalized industry-wide, and metrics produced in the first reporting cycle will reflect inconsistent 
interpretations of new categorical definitions. Public posting of data derived from immature, first-cycle 
implementation would undermine transparency by presenting figures based on varying interpretations of 
new definitions.  
Prior CMS transparency rulemaking history confirms that adequate ramp-up time is essential for reliable 
reporting outputs. Programs launched with compressed implementation windows have produced 
incomplete or inconsistent reporting that the agency has subsequently had to address through corrective

publicly reported cycle accurately reflects substantive PA performance rather than first-cycle

We recommend CMS extend the compliance date for public posting of drug PA metrics to provide 
impacted payers adequate time to operationalize the new reporting framework. In the alternative, 
CMS should exercise enforcement discretion with respect to public posting during the first 
reporting cycle following the ruleâ€™s effective date. 
B. An Avoided-PA Measure for Pharmacy Benefit Drug Authorization Would Provide Meaningful 
Insight Into Upstream Modernization Investment 
The metrics enumerated in the Proposed Rule (i.e., approvals, denials, decision time, extensions, and 
appeals) capture the volume and disposition of prior authorization requests that enter the formal PA 
process. This is appropriate and useful. However, the current metric set does not capture an important 
dimension of how modernized payer operations have been deployed in the pharmacy-benefit drug PA 
context, specifically: the upstream deflection of PA requirements through point-of-prescribing decision 
support and benefit transparency tools. 
In the drug PA context, payers and pharmacy benefit managers have invested in technology 
infrastructure that allows coverage decisions to be communicated to prescribers at the point of 
prescribing. This infrastructure includes real-time benefit checks via NCPDP RTPB, formulary intelligence 
delivered through NCPDP F&B, and e-prescribing alerts triggered by NCPDP SCRIPT integration with 
EHR systems. When functioning effectively, these tools allow many coverage determinations to be 
resolved at the point of prescribing without ever entering the formal PA workflow, because the prescriber 
receives benefit information sufficient to select an alternative or to proceed with the original prescription 
based on confirmed coverage. The very same NCPDP standards CMS proposes to adopt in this rule are 
designed in part to enable this upstream resolution. 
Prime recognizes that the operational mechanisms enabling upstream PA deflection are unique to the 
drug-benefit context. The point-of-prescribing infrastructure, specifically real-time benefit checks (NCPDP 
RTPB), formulary intelligence (NCPDP F&B), and e-prescribing decision support (NCPDP SCRIPT) 
provides a mature framework for real-time intervention that currently lacks a direct technical parallel in 
the medical-benefit workflow.

While pharmacy standards allow for automated, measurable deflection at the point of care, medical-
benefit authorizations involve different stakeholders, different timing, and an entirely different technical 
infrastructure (typically HL7 FHIR or X12). 
Therefore, Prime recommends that CMS: 
â€¢ 
Limit these measures to drug PA: Apply the measurement of upstream deflection only where 
the NCPDP infrastructure makes such tracking operationally feasible. 
â€¢ 
Exclude medical-benefit PA: Refrain from extending these requirements to medical services, as 
the lack of standardized "real-time service checks" would create a significant administrative 
burden and result in inconsistent data. 
A measure capturing systematically avoided PAs in the pharmacy-benefit drug PA context would provide 
CMS, plan beneficiaries, prescribers, and policymakers with insight into how effectively impacted payers 
have deployed point-of-prescribing modernization investment; insight that the current metric set does not 
provide. Prime acknowledges that the operational definition of such a measure requires industry 
collaboration to develop, including consensus on counting mechanisms (per 1,000 prescriptions for PA-
required drugs, per member-month, or another denominator), data source attribution, and reporting 
cadence. We do not recommend immediate adoption without that collaboration. 
We recommend CMS engage stakeholders including impacted payers, pharmacy benefit 
managers, standards-development organizations, and prescriber and consumer representatives 
to develop an operational definition for a pharmacy benefit avoided-PA measure as a utilization-
management effectiveness indicator. We further recommend that such a measure, once defined, 
be incorporated into the drug PA reporting framework in a future rulemaking cycle as a 
complement to the metrics in the current Proposed Rule. 
V. Conclusion 
Prime appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments on the Proposed Rule. We support CMS's 
movement toward modernizing drug prior authorization and advancing interoperability across the payer 
landscape. The recommendations above are offered with the goal of ensuring that CMS's regulatory 
framework supports practical, durable implementation that delivers meaningful results for plan 
beneficiaries, prescribers, and impacted payers. 
In summary, Prime requests that CMS: 
â€¢ Extend the compliance date for medical-benefit drug PA integration into the FHIR Prior Authorization 
API to allow sufficient lead time between finalization of the drug prior authorization implementation 
requirements and required compliance. 
â€¢ Calibrate NCPDP standards adoption to ecosystem readiness, including a phased compliance 
approach that maintains the proposed timeline for Medicare Part D and QHP programs while 
providing at least 24 additional months for Medicaid and CHIP RTPB implementation; 
â€¢ Clarify that drug PA decision timeframes begin upon receipt of all information necessary for a 
determination, rather than upon initial receipt of the request; and

analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Prime Therapeutics LLC; signed by Steve Cutts, PharmD, Senior Vice President and Chief Clinical and Specialty Officer.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor / PBM / Payer operations vendor.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Prime describes itself as a pharmacy solutions partner providing pharmacy benefit management, specialty and medical drug management, and state government solutions to millions of people.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Prime supports CMS's movement toward electronic prior authorization and drug interoperability standards, but asks CMS to align compliance timing and reporting requirements with operational readiness. Its main recommendations are to extend the medical-benefit drug FHIR API compliance timeline, phase Medicaid/CHIP RTPB implementation, start PA decision clocks only after receipt of all necessary information, delay first-cycle public reporting of drug PA metrics, and develop an avoided-PA pharmacy-benefit metric through stakeholder collaboration.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; CMS-0057-F; Proposed section II.B.3; Proposed section II.A.2; Proposed sections II.A.2.a, II.B.4; Proposed sections II.A.2.b, II.B.5; Proposed sections II.A.2.c, II.B.6; Proposed section II.C.3; Proposed section II.C.7.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR Prior Authorization API; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP Formulary and Benefit (F&B) Version 60; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) Version 13; Da Vinci PDex 2.1.0; CARIN Blue Button 2.2.0; HL7 FHIR; X12; EHR integrations.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Medical-benefit drug PA integration into FHIR API**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Prime supports the FHIR API policy but says medical-benefit drug PA is newly added and requires drug-specific implementation guidance, client responsibility alignment, engineering work, and complex benefit categorization.
- **Specific request:** Extend compliance to no earlier than 15 months after final implementation guidance, or provide first-year enforcement discretion.

**Topic 2: NCPDP standards and ecosystem readiness**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** Prime supports SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB but says ecosystem readiness differs by standard and line of business, especially outside Part D.
- **Specific request:** Support SCRIPT broadly; publish detailed F&B implementation guidance with lead time and allow backward-compatible version updates without full rulemaking; phase RTPB compliance by keeping October 1, 2027 for Part D and QHPs but adding 24 months for Medicaid and CHIP.

**Topic 3: Drug PA decision clock start**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify.
- **Rationale:** Prime supports shorter decision durations but says many requests are incomplete and ultimately approved after outreach, so starting the clock at initial receipt could force unnecessary denials and appeals.
- **Specific request:** Start the decision timeframe when the impacted payer receives all information necessary for a determination, rather than initial receipt of the request.

**Topic 4: Public drug PA metric reporting timing**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** Prime supports transparency but argues new categorical definitions, aggregation rules, and data flows need time before reliable public reporting.
- **Specific request:** Extend the compliance date for public posting of drug PA metrics, or exercise enforcement discretion during the first reporting cycle.

**Topic 5: Avoided-PA measure for pharmacy benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify/future addition.
- **Rationale:** Current metrics capture formal PA requests but not PA requirements avoided through RTPB, F&B, SCRIPT, and point-of-prescribing decision support.
- **Specific request:** Convene impacted payers, PBMs, SDOs, prescribers, and consumer representatives to define a pharmacy-benefit avoided-PA metric for future rulemaking; limit the measure to pharmacy-benefit drug PA and exclude medical-benefit PA because comparable real-time infrastructure does not exist.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S2/S3:** Addresses IG and standards version management, recommending flexibility for backward-compatible updates and a streamlined recognition process to avoid outdated regulatory version locks.
- **S12:** Identifies medical-benefit drug FHIR API implementation challenges, including 9-15 months of build effort, up to  million in IT investment, drug categorization complexity, and risk of misrouted requests or denials.
- **S14:** Supports NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB for pharmacy benefit drugs but asks CMS to calibrate implementation by standard and program readiness.
- **S19:** Directly raises state Medicaid readiness concerns for RTPB due to PDL variation, supplemental rebates, MCO carve-outs, and safety-net provider EHR fragmentation.
- **S21:** Says the October 1, 2027 medical-benefit drug PA API date is operationally challenging and asks for at least 15 months after final guidance.
- **S22:** Cites substantial IT costs and implementation work for medical-benefit drug PA and ecosystem-wide NCPDP alignment.
- **S25:** States RTPB is mature in Medicare Part D but materially less mature in Medicaid and CHIP, requiring a phased timeline.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Supports public drug PA metrics but asks for delayed first-cycle posting/enforcement discretion and future development of an avoided-PA measure.
- **S37:** Addresses implementation challenges across payers, vendors, EHRs, PBMs, and standards alignment.
- **S44-S56:** Does not directly address HIPAA authority, but notes medical-benefit workflows involve HL7 FHIR or X12 and should not be conflated with pharmacy-benefit NCPDP workflows.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Extend medical-benefit drug PA FHIR Prior Authorization API compliance to at least 15 months after final implementation guidance.
2. Provide first-year enforcement discretion if CMS does not extend the medical-benefit drug API compliance date.
3. Support NCPDP SCRIPT across pharmacy-benefit lines of business.
4. Publish detailed NCPDP F&B implementation guidance, including version specifications and compatibility requirements, with sufficient lead time.
5. Avoid overly granular regulatory version-locking by allowing backward-compatible standard updates or streamlined recognition of newer versions.
6. Adopt a phased RTPB timeline: full compliance for Part D and QHPs by October 1, 2027, and 24 additional months for Medicaid and CHIP.
7. Clarify that drug PA decision clocks begin when all information necessary for determination is received.
8. Extend the public drug PA metrics posting compliance date or use first-cycle enforcement discretion.
9. Engage stakeholders to define a pharmacy-benefit avoided-PA metric as a future utilization-management effectiveness indicator.
10. Do not extend avoided-PA measurement requirements to medical-benefit services or medical-benefit PA absent comparable standardized real-time infrastructure.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Operational timeline feasibility, ecosystem readiness, standards version-locking, Medicaid/CHIP RTPB readiness, incomplete PA submissions, first-cycle reporting inconsistency, and inappropriate extension of pharmacy-specific measures to medical benefit workflows.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Misrouted PA requests, misapplied coverage logic, delayed beneficiary access, inappropriate denials, disrupted therapy, denials followed by avoidable appeals, inaccurate public reporting, and technical compliance without functional transparency.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Drug benefit categorization by route and coverage logic, health plan-client operational responsibility alignment, payer/vendor/EHR coordination, Medicaid PDL and rebate variation, MCO carve-outs, safety-net provider EHR gaps, provider response times, and lack of medical-benefit real-time service-check infrastructure.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Prime estimates medical-benefit drug PA FHIR API implementation requires 9-15 months of build effort and up to  million in IT investment. Prime reports average pharmacy benefit drug PA decision time of about 0.57 days/13.7 hours from May 2025-May 2026. It reports that approximately 15 percent of Medicaid reviews and 30 percent of Medicare reviews from January-May 2026 required outbound research, and that 35 percent of those Medicaid cases and 37 percent of those Medicare cases were granted after outreach.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not external studies; relies primarily on Prime operational experience and data.
- **Examples provided:** Medical-benefit drugs administered through different routes triggering different benefit categories; Medicaid RTPB readiness affected by state PDLs, supplemental rebates, MCO carve-outs, low cost-sharing, and safety-net provider EHR gaps; point-of-prescribing avoided PA through RTPB/F&B/SCRIPT.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** PBMs, impacted payers, health plan clients, state Medicaid and CHIP programs, QHPs, Medicare Part D plans, prescribers, EHR vendors, SDOs, beneficiaries, and safety-net practices.
- **Economic implications:** Prime identifies up to  million in IT investment for medical-benefit drug PA API implementation and potential costs from misrouting, appeals, duplicate work, and unreliable reporting.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible with adequate lead time, final guidance, version flexibility, ecosystem testing, phased Medicaid/CHIP RTPB adoption, and careful metric definition. Risky if CMS applies uniform deadlines to immature ecosystems.
- **Patient care impact:** Prime frames its requested changes as preventing delayed medication access, inappropriate denials, disrupted ongoing therapy, and avoidable denial/appeal cycles.
